t: A Shona kingdom on the Zimbabwe plateau, ruled from Great Zimbabwe, which grew rich on cattle and on gold and ivory sent to the coast at Sofala.
Its dry-stone walls, up to 11 metres high in the Great Enclosure, are the largest precolonial stone structures in southern Africa.
Power passed to the Mutapa and Butua states after about 1450, but the ruins gave the modern nation of Zimbabwe its name and emblem.
dyk: The Zimbabwe Bird on the national flag copies soapstone carvings from the ruins; one was taken by a hunter in 1889 and sold to Cecil Rhodes, and four were returned from South Africa in 1981.
ev: Farming communities settle the hill at Great Zimbabwe
Builders begin enclosing the Hill Complex with dry-stone walls
The Great Enclosure and its conical tower are built south of the hill
Great Zimbabwe loses its role as the Mutapa and Butua states rise
Vicente Pegado, captain at Sofala, records the name ‘Symbaoe’ for the stone buildings
Karl Mauch visits the ruins and attributes them to the Queen of Sheba
Gertrude Caton-Thompson’s excavations confirm the site’s African and medieval origin
Independent Zimbabwe takes its name from the ruins

f.predecessor: Gumanye farming communities; Kingdom of Mapungubwe
